newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Hundreds join anti-India protest in Bangladesh.
newsitem.headline: Hundreds join anti-India protest in Bangladesh.

text.p: Hundreds of opposition party activists party staged a noisy anti-India demonstration in Dhaka on Friday, accusing Bangladesh's giant neighbour of attempting a cultural and political invasion.

The protesters, organised by the Jatiya Ganotantrik Party (JAGPA), called for the end of a week-long India festival now on in Dhaka and other cities and for the sending back home of Jyoti Basu, chief minister of India's West Bengal state.
Basu is visiting Bangladesh for talks on sharing water from the River Ganges.
Bangladeshi and Indian officials said they were hopeful the two countries would be able to sign a water deal in December, ending a decades-old dispute.
Jatiya chief Shafiul Alam Pradhan told reporters Basu's visit was intended to exert political pressure on Bangladesh to allow India to transport goods to its northeastern states through Bangladesh.

"Giving India a transit and pursuing Bangladesh's plan to buy electricity from India would both be suicidal," he said. "India is a hegemonist power and may try to undermine Bangladesh's sovereignty by using its increased influence."
Power-starved Bangladesh has announced plans to buy electricity from neighbouring countries.
One protester said India was trying to "invade Bangladesh's very rich and distinctive culture".
"The ongoing India festival is clear proof of that. It displays many things which are not compatible with local culture," he said.
Members of several Moslem groups also protested against New Delhi.
"Bangladesh is essentially a Moslem country which has ensured religious harmony and peaceful co-existence for all communities," said a Moslem leader during an anti-India rally.
"But that does not mean we will accept anything from India and open up everything of Bangladesh to India."

The Moslem groups and the JAGPA were echoing warnings by the main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party, headed by former prime minister Khaleda Zia, that "too much closeness" to India might jeopardise Bangladesh's independence.
India and then west Pakistan went to war over the founding of Bangladesh, formerly East Pakistan, in 1971.
